claim: The US-ANSI physical keyboard layout uses a horizontal Return key that is 2.25u wide with the backslash key directly above it.
excerpt: The US-ANSI keyboard layout (ANSI-INCITS 154-1988) has a horizontal Return key with the \ key above it. It is often 2.25u wide.

claim: The ISO and JIS keyboard standards specify a vertical Return key spanning two rows that is typically 1.25u wide.
excerpt: The ISO standard (ISO/IEC 9995-2) mandates a vertical Return key spanning two rows. The Japanese JIS standard (JIS X 6002-1980) uses the same key as ISO. It is often 1.25u wide.

claim: A backwards L-shaped or Big-Ass Enter key combines the area of both ANSI and ISO Return keys and requires relocating adjacent keys.
excerpt: A "backwards-L shaped" (or just "L-shaped") Return key is the union of the ISO and ANSI Return keys. The key is often called Big-ass Enter because of its size, or Asian enter because it is found on many East Asian keyboards.

claim: Standard ANSI PC keyboards feature 101 keys for legacy full-size, 104 keys for modern full-size with OS keys, or 87 keys for tenkeyless.
excerpt: PC keyboards using the ANSI layout as used by the IBM Model M are typically referred to as 101-key (pre-1995), 104-key (with the Windows and context menu keys added), and 87-key (standard tenkeyless layout).

claim: ISO keyboards contain one additional physical key compared to ANSI layouts, giving key counts of 102, 105, or 88 keys.
excerpt: ISO keyboards are used by many European countries, and with one extra key compared to ANSI keyboards, are correspondingly referred to as 102-key, 105-key and 88-key for PCs.

claim: JIS keyboards contain four more physical keys than ISO and five more than ANSI, typically yielding 109 keys on full-size boards.
excerpt: With Windows keys, they are typically referred to as 109-key: they have four more keys compared to ISO, and five more keys compared to ANSI.

claim: Physical keyboard format standards like ANSI and ISO define board geometry independently from software keymaps and keycap legends.

source.title: Which countries use a QWERTY keyboard layout? – Krome Keyboards

excerpt: Physical format is separate from language layout. ANSI, ISO, JIS and ABNT describe a keyboard’s shape and key count, not the software language assigned to it. An ISO keyboard body can carry a QWERTY layout just as easily as a QWERTZ one.

claim: European language layouts adapt the core ISO physical standard by modifying keycap legends or adding physical keys for regional characters.

source.title: Which countries use a QWERTY keyboard layout? – Krome Keyboards

excerpt: European languages have adapted the core arrangement to accommodate characters absent from the 26-letter English alphabet. Some variants add physical keys, while others use the AltGr key for accented or specialised characters

claim: Standard key switch unit pitch in mechanical keyboard layout design is 19.05 mm (0.75 inches).
excerpt: The Rafi full-travel keyswitches RS 76 are modular systems for designing individual key blocks and keyboards in the 3/4 inch (= 19.05 mm) grid.

claim: Keys sized 2u and larger require mechanical stabilizers to prevent wobbling and ensure even vertical travel.
excerpt: Wider keys (2u and above, like spacebar, backspace, left shift, and enter) would wobble if held only by their switch. Stabilizers are mechanical brackets that clip onto the PCB and keep both ends of the key moving evenly. You only need stabilizers for keys that are 2u or wider.

claim: Key stabilizers utilize a stiff wire spanning between keycap mounts to force level key movement and prevent binding on wide keycaps.
excerpt: A stiff wire runs from one end of the key to the other, connected to the keycap at each end, and to the keyboard plate or PCB via some form of restraint.

claim: PCB-mounted Cherry MX stabilizers attach through four PCB mounting holes (two per side) per stabilized key.
excerpt: PCB-mount Cherry MX levelling mechanisms clip into the PCB. The PCB contains four holes, two per side; the rear stabiliser legs allow it to be swung into place via the rear holes, and prongs in the front place grip the front holes.

claim: Cherry MX style PCB-mount stabilizer assemblies are sized in standard 2u, 6.25u, and 7u wire classes.

claim: Non-standard keyboard form factors are governed by community conventions rather than formal standards, dividing into ortholinear, columnar stagger, and compact 40% layouts.
excerpt: Ortholinear keyboards, on the other hand, are organized in a grid like fashion where all keys form 90deg corners with all other keys. Columnar staggered keyboards are keyboards where the columns are offset from each other.

claim: JIS physical layouts incorporate a single-unit backspace, shortened spacebar, and reduced-width right shift with an adjacent additional key.
excerpt: Common features to Japanese keyboards are the single-unit backspace, reduced width right shift with additional key (on the opposite side to where ISO adds a key beside shift) and vertical enter. The space bar is greatly reduced in width however remains to be still in centre position.
